title: Tracer-calibrated near-outcrop ventilation gives North Pacific sigma0 26.5 AOU gains of observed size (1984-2025); early 160-170 E gain needs the 1985-2004 flow change; California keeps an excess
abstract: Question: does weaker ventilation, calculated from where the winter surface of the North Pacific (NP) became lighter and how the flow changed, explain the size, timing and pattern of the AOU gains on sigma0 26.5 in 1984-2025? Approach: a two-dimensional advection-diffusion model on the 26.5 surface with WOA23 geostrophic flow and WOA23 decadal late-winter surface density (1955-2022), calibrated with CFC-12/SF6 transit-time ages from four Pacific sections, not with the change data. We compared it with observed AOU gains (2009-2025 minus 1984-1996) in 7 regions from World Ocean Database ship data. Results: ventilation only where the winter surface is denser than 26.5 gave ages 4-6 times too old. With ventilation also where the winter surface is near 26.5, the ages agreed within a factor of about 1.5. With fixed flow and tracer OUR, 8 equally good parameter sets gave gains of 18-49 umol/kg at 160-170 E (observed 18), 10-46 in the transition zone (observed 34.5) and 9-19 off California (observed 23.9). Most of the change came from the lighter winter surface south of 45 N at 165 E-165 W. An OUR that increases where 26.5 is shallow (fitted to the WOA23 AOU map) explained most of the east-west pattern; with one scale factor set by the other regions, California still had 1.2-1.8 times the predicted gain. With fixed flow the rise at 160-170 E came too late (12% before 2006; observed 59%). The stronger Kuroshio Extension recirculation of 1985-2004 in WOA23 gave the early rise (49-79%). Limitations: one isopycnal, smoothed decadal fields with few data before 1985, equally good parameter sets that differ by a factor of about 3 in sensitivity, a fixed southern boundary with uncertain age, constant OUR, and post hoc pattern and OUR tests.
